question: Why does the rupee keep falling, and does it actually make you poorer?

theme.label: Economy and public money
readerQuestions: What is the headline economic number?
Is this a total number or a per-person number?
How much of the story is prices, exchange rates, or GDP share?
What does this explain about household life?

plannedCharts.title: From four rupees to ninety
plannedCharts.subtitle: What one US dollar has cost in rupees since Independence: flat for decades under fixed pegs, then stepping down through each devaluation.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The headline everyone knows and almost everyone misreads: the rupee's long slide against the dollar.

plannedCharts.title: The fall, decade by decade
plannedCharts.unit: % of value lost vs the dollar
plannedCharts.subtitle: How much of its dollar value the rupee gave up in each decade. The losses came in bursts, not a steady slide.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The slide was never steady; it came in bursts, and naming the decades shows the rupee has been broadly stable against the dollar for long stretches.

plannedCharts.title: Did the rupee fall, or did the dollar rise?
plannedCharts.subtitle: The rupee's value against four big currencies since 1999. It slid most against the dollar, far less against the pound and yen.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The rupee did not weaken evenly against everything; it fell hardest against the dollar and far less against the pound and yen, so much of the 'weakness' is really dollar strength.

plannedCharts.title: The rupee was not alone
plannedCharts.unit: % of value lost vs the dollar, 2000-2025
plannedCharts.subtitle: How far every major currency fell against a strong dollar since 2000. The rupee sits mid-pack, not among the worst.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The most freeing chart in the article: a currency's price is relative, and against a strong dollar most currencies lost ground, with the rupee sitting mid-pack among emerging markets, far from the worst.

plannedCharts.title: From a fortnight of imports to over six hundred billion dollars
plannedCharts.subtitle: India's stockpile of foreign currency and gold. This buffer shrank to almost nothing in 1991 and now ranks among the world's largest.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The 1991 devaluation was not a choice, it was a near-default: India had almost run out of dollars.

plannedCharts.title: The deficit that sets off every crisis
plannedCharts.subtitle: India's current-account balance, the gap between what the country earns abroad and what it spends. It turns into a dollar squeeze whenever foreign money stops coming.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Behind every rupee crisis is the same trigger: India spending more abroad than it earns, so it must pull in foreign money to bridge the gap, and when that money stops, the rupee breaks.

plannedCharts.title: The price of money, through every regime
plannedCharts.subtitle: The RBI's main interest rate over the decades: towering in the controlled era, spiking to defend the rupee in crises, calmer today.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The interest-rate backdrop to the whole story: sky-high in the controlled era, spiking to defend the rupee in crises, low and steadier today.

plannedCharts.title: The rupee's monthly trading range
plannedCharts.subtitle: The highest and lowest the rupee touched within each month. The band is so tight it reveals how much the RBI smooths the currency.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A genuine free float would swing wildly; the rupee's tight monthly band is the fingerprint of management.

plannedCharts.title: What the RBI actually does in the market
plannedCharts.subtitle: How many dollars the RBI bought or sold each month: buying to hold the rupee down in calm times, selling hard to defend it in a crisis.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The central bank says it only curbs volatility; its dollar buying and selling shows what that means month to month.

plannedCharts.title: The tide the central bank leans against
plannedCharts.subtitle: Foreign investors' stock-and-bond flows alongside the RBI's dollar trades. When hot money rushes out, the RBI sells dollars to cushion the fall.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: RBI research finds the rupee is moved mainly by volatile foreign portfolio flows, not by inflation; intervention leans against that tide.

plannedCharts.title: The hundred-billion-dollar shadow defence
plannedCharts.subtitle: The RBI's hidden forward position: dollars it has promised to deliver later, a way to defend the rupee today without spending visible reserves.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Modern intervention increasingly hides in the forwards market, off the visible spot reserves.

plannedCharts.title: Patient money and hot money
plannedCharts.subtitle: Sticky factory-building investment against fast-moving stock-market money. It is the second kind that whipsaws the rupee.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Not all foreign money behaves the same: direct investment is sticky and builds factories, portfolio money is fast and can leave in a week, and it is the second kind that whipsaws the rupee.

plannedCharts.title: What really moves the rupee
plannedCharts.subtitle: When the dollar strengthens against all emerging markets, the rupee falls with the pack. The two lines mirror each other.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The rupee's worst stretches line up with a globally strong dollar, not with India-specific news: when the dollar rises against all emerging markets, the rupee falls with the pack.

plannedCharts.title: How tightly the RBI actually held the rupee
plannedCharts.subtitle: The rupee against the dollar, split into the RBI's unspoken regimes. The labels mark how freely it was allowed to move: the steadier the line, the tighter the grip.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The clearest 'words versus deeds' evidence: the RBI never announces how hard it is managing the rupee, but how much the rupee moves in each regime gives it away.

plannedCharts.title: The rupee collapsed. Or did it?
plannedCharts.subtitle: The rupee three ways since 1994: crashing against the dollar, falling less on a trade-weighted basis, and almost flat once inflation is stripped out.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The single chart that overturns the panic: against the dollar the rupee fell to a third, but in real trade-weighted terms it barely moved.

plannedCharts.title: The real rupee across fifty years
plannedCharts.subtitle: The rupee's inflation-adjusted value since 1975: overvalued under the old pegs, sharply corrected in 1991, then broadly stable.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Zoom out to half a century and the real rupee tells a story of correction, not collapse.

plannedCharts.title: Why the rupee had to fall

series.label: Cost of living in the US

plannedCharts.subtitle: The cost of living in India versus the US since 1991. India's climbs far higher, and that gap is roughly what the rupee had to give up.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The engine under the whole story: since 1991 Indian prices have risen far more than American prices, and a currency cannot hold a fixed dollar value while its prices outrun the other country's.

plannedCharts.title: How much of the fall is just inflation?
plannedCharts.subtitle: The actual rupee-dollar rate against the rate inflation alone would justify. Inflation explains most of the fall, but the rupee overshoots it.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Inflation differences explain the direction of the fall, but not all of it, and the gap is the honest part of the story.

plannedCharts.title: Why a higher-inflation currency drifts down
plannedCharts.subtitle: Year-on-year inflation in India and the US. India's has sat above America's for decades, the gap the rupee keeps having to offset.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The mechanism under the whole story: India has run higher inflation than the US for decades, so the rupee must fall to keep trade competitive.

plannedCharts.title: Is the rupee just a number?
plannedCharts.subtitle: The same Indian exports measured in rupees and in dollars. The rupee line looks like a miracle, and the gap between them is purely the exchange rate.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The same exports look like a miracle in rupees and a steady climb in dollars; the entire gap is the exchange rate.

plannedCharts.title: Did you actually lose money?

series.label: One rupee in a bank deposit

plannedCharts.subtitle: One rupee left in a bank deposit since 1970 against the rising cost of living. The saved rupee stays ahead; cash under the mattress loses almost everything.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The reframe that defuses the debasement panic: nobody holds wealth in cash, and a banked rupee kept its purchasing power.

plannedCharts.title: When even the bank lost to inflation
plannedCharts.subtitle: What a bank deposit paid after subtracting inflation. Negative through the repression decades, reliably positive only after the 1990s reforms.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The honest other half of the savings story: in the controlled decades the interest a deposit paid was less than inflation, so even the careful saver lost ground, until liberalisation turned real rates positive.

plannedCharts.title: Why petrol hurts more here
plannedCharts.subtitle: The price of crude oil in dollars and in rupees since 2000. The rupee line climbs higher because a weaker currency stacks on top of the world price.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India imports most of its oil in dollars, so a weaker rupee raises the pump price even when world oil is flat.

plannedCharts.title: The petroleum bill the rupee has to pay
plannedCharts.subtitle: India's annual bill for imported oil, its single biggest dollar outflow and the main way a weak rupee feeds straight into inflation.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Oil is India's single biggest import and the main reason a weak rupee feeds straight into inflation.

plannedCharts.title: The dollar debt a weak rupee makes heavier
plannedCharts.subtitle: Dollar-denominated debt owed by Indian companies and other non-banks. A weaker rupee raises the rupee cost of repaying it, which is what bit unhedged borrowers in the 2013 panic.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Beyond importers and travellers, a weak rupee squeezes borrowers who owe in dollars: the dollar figure is flat but the rupee bill rises.

plannedCharts.title: The other side: a weak rupee pays the diaspora more
plannedCharts.subtitle: The money Indians abroad send home each year. A falling rupee quietly turns each of those dollars into more rupees for families.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Depreciation is not all cost: India is the world's largest remittance recipient, and every weaker rupee turns each sent dollar into more rupees at home.

plannedCharts.title: Why India always needs more dollars
plannedCharts.subtitle: India's exports against its imports. The country buys more from the world than it sells, so it is forever in need of dollars.
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Underneath the currency sits a simple fact: India buys more from the world than it sells, so it constantly needs dollars, which is why capital flows and remittances matter so much.

Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.

If source coverage is thin, say so directly.

forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
